claims.text: A brief sub-glass-transition isothermal anneal immediately after rapid quenching improves the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
The post-quench sub-Tg anneal improves the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
Sub-Tg annealing reduces internal free volume in the amorphous alloy.
Sub-Tg annealing produces a more uniform short-range atomic arrangement or local chemical order.
Atomic rearrangements during sub-Tg annealing relieve internal stresses.
A properly selected sub-Tg anneal permits structural relaxation without supplying enough energy for crystalline nucleation and growth.
The annealed alloy will resist crystallization better than the otherwise identical as-quenched alloy during subsequent heating.
Improved resistance to crystallization will appear as a delayed crystallization-onset temperature in DSC.
The beneficial treatment is limited to a narrow window of sub-Tg annealing temperatures and hold times.
An annealing temperature or duration that is too high or too long can cause premature phase transformation or crystallization.
An annealing temperature or duration that is too low or too short will provide insufficient free-volume relaxation.
The intervention may fail for compositions having particularly small glass-transition stability margins.
The optimal annealing temperature depends on alloy composition.
The optimal annealing time and temperature depend on the preceding cooling conditions.

contradictions.description: The intervention is performed only after the alloy has already been quenched into an amorphous state, yet it is claimed to improve glass-forming ability, which concerns formation of the glass during cooling. The predicted outcomes and experiment assess only post-formation crystallization resistance and therefore do not operationalize or test the claimed improvement in glass-forming ability.
